title: Drop-Then-Recovery: How Redundant Are Vision-Language-Action Models?
action_head: mixed: flow/diffusion action expert (pi0.5, Lingbot-VLA, GigaBrain-0) and regression head (OpenVLA-OFT MLP head)
methods: Drop-Then-Recovery: physically remove transformer blocks, then recovery fine-tune
fixed component interventions (Drop Half, Keep 2) for vision, language, action
GateProbe: gradient of action loss w.r.t. a virtual residual gate per block
comparison with CosSim, magnitude, perplexity, Taylor, IGIA metrics
granularity comparison (block vs MHA vs MLP)
question: How much of each VLA component (vision, language, action) is needed for closed-loop control once the model is allowed to recover by fine-tuning?
key_findings: Strong asymmetry: on LIBERO, OpenVLA-OFT with half its LLM blocks removed reaches 98.3% vs 95.0% baseline after recovery, while dropping half the vision blocks (3.6% of parameters) falls to 83.9%; on pi0.5, Keep-2 for vision or action collapses to 62.4% and 26.2%, while Keep-2 for language stays near baseline.
Keeping only two language blocks recovers baseline-level success (OpenVLA-OFT 95.1%, pi0.5 91.0% vs 91.7%); FLOPs-matched pi0.5 Drop-12 reaches 93.7% (+2.0), Drop-17 (one language block) 91.0%.
Whole-block dropping beats sublayer dropping on OpenVLA-OFT (98.3% vs MHA 91.9% vs MLP 65.6%); on pi0.5 all granularities give 93.3-94.1%.
GateProbe is best or second-best at four drop levels on pi0.5, with larger margins under aggressive removal (+3.9 at Drop-16, +4.3 at Drop-17).

Redundancy is not free under shift: at Drop-9, LIBERO-Plus drops 3.8 points overall, with the largest loss on robot initial-pose perturbations (-10.6) rather than language (-5.1); RoboTwin 2.0 Hard variants lose 6.6 points vs 0.6 on Easy.

Real xArm 850 parcel sorting with pi0.5 (3 runs x 20 grasps): Env 1 full 63.3%, Drop-9 65.0%, Drop-16 55.0%; Env 2 full 75.0%, Drop-9 71.7%, Drop-16 66.7%; dropped models are less robust under six OOD conditions.
Without recovery, zero-shot dropping is slower end-to-end (e.g. 0.72x task speedup at 78% success) because failures add steps; DTR-16 gives 1.64x task speedup and 42% less memory on OpenVLA-OFT.

evidence.setting: both (LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0 simulation; xArm 850 real robot)
evidence.scale: LIBERO: 20 trials per task (main), some tables 10 tasks x 5 trials with one seed; real robot 3 runs x 20 grasps per condition
evidence.baselines: full fine-tuned models under matched training compute; static and gradient-based block importance metrics; zero-shot dropping; quantization and 2:4 pruning in appendix

causal_validation: Yes in the ablation sense: blocks are removed and closed-loop success measured. But because every dropped model is re-fine-tuned, the protocol measures whether capacity is necessary for the task distribution, not what the original model's blocks compute.
closed_loop: Yes, all success rates are closed-loop rollouts in simulation and on the real robot.
limitations_stated: Redundancy reflects current benchmarks, which use short templated instructions; removed language blocks still matter for robustness to physical perturbations and harder tasks.
In pi0.5, dropping a language block removes only about 75% of its parameters because K/V projections must stay for the action expert's joint attention.
critique: For pi0.5 the 'language block removal' keeps that layer's K/V projections, which are then retrained as cross-attention adapters on an identity-passed hidden state; so the result shows the action expert can be re-conditioned on shallow features, not that backbone computation is irrelevant. This connects to the narrow interface found causally in 2610.20750.

Recovery fine-tuning on LIBERO, a near-saturated benchmark, makes over-capacity easy to show; the LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin Hard drops are the more informative numbers and point the other way for deployment.
20 trials per task, no seeds or CIs, so gains like 95.0 -> 98.3 are within plausible noise.
Consistent with other batch papers that find weak language dependence on LIBERO (2603.06001, 2610.10178, 2604.18000), from an architectural angle.
one_line: Removing most language-backbone blocks from pi0.5, OpenVLA-OFT and other VLAs and re-fine-tuning keeps LIBERO success near or above baseline, while removing vision or action blocks breaks them, suggesting current benchmarks barely need the language model, though robustness to physical shifts suffers.
